title: Fraud Detection and Forensics
answer: Expense fraud, money laundering networks, vendor fraud, communication forensics and tracing digital assets.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Expense Fraud
children.blurb: Expense fraud covers claims that are false, inflated, duplicated or outside policy, from a fabricated taxi receipt to a supplier invoice routed through an employee's own account.

children.name: Money Laundering Networks
children.blurb: Money laundering networks are the webs of accounts, shell companies, intermediaries and counterparties used to move the proceeds of crime so their origin is obscured.

children.name: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
children.blurb: Phantom vendors and procurement fraud covers the creation of fake suppliers, shell companies, or inflated invoices that divert an organisation's money to an insider or an outside colluder.

children.name: Communication Forensics
children.blurb: Communication forensics is the examination of messages, calls, emails and documents to establish who said what, when, and whether the record can be trusted.

children.name: Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets
children.blurb: Tracing and recovering digital assets covers the work of following value as it moves through bank ledgers, card networks, payment processors, exchange accounts, wallets and internal accounting systems, then trying to get it back.

sections.body: Fraud detection and forensics is the work of finding money that was taken, hidden, or invented, and of building a record that stands up to scrutiny. In accounting, artificial intelligence is now used to scan expense reports for patterns a human reviewer would miss, to link transactions across accounts and entities that appear unrelated, and to flag vendors that exist only on paper. It reads language as well as numbers, so it can sort through emails, chat logs, and contracts for signs of collusion or pressure. The aim is not to replace the investigator but to narrow the pile of records worth a closer look. What the machine produces is a lead, and a person still decides what it means.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The strongest results are in high volume, repetitive screening, where models are good at ranking anomalies and poor at explaining them. Expense anomalies and duplicate invoices are largely a solved screening problem, though false positives remain common and costly in staff time. Money laundering is harder because the networks adapt, and a model trained on last year's typologies can miss next year's. Communication forensics has improved with language models, but attributing a message to a person is still contested ground. Tracing digital assets is technically feasible on public ledgers and much harder once funds pass through mixers, exchanges, or jurisdictions that do not cooperate. Nothing here is legal or financial advice, and no output should be treated as proof on its own.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from the smallest unit of loss to the hardest to recover. Expense Fraud covers the everyday case, employee claims and receipts, and is the natural starting point for how anomaly detection works in practice. Money Laundering Networks widens the view to flows between accounts and entities, where graph methods and network analysis matter more than single transactions. Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud sits between the two, covering fake suppliers and bid rigging, and shows how records and communications have to be read together. Communication Forensics takes up that second thread, the language evidence in emails, chats, and documents. Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets is the end of the chain, following funds onto ledgers and through exchanges, and it is the page to read when the question is where the money went rather than how it left.
